COMBINED SCIENCE O-LEVEL — ZIMSEC STUDY GUIDE

This offline Study Pack is designed around the ZIMSEC O-Level Combined Science examination subject code 4003 and the official examination components. ZIMSEC official resources list Combined Science 4003/01, 4003/02 and 4003/03, including multiple-choice, theory and practical components.

CURRICULUM ORGANISATION
The Study Pack integrates Biology, Chemistry and Physics together with practical scientific investigation, data handling, technology/robotics applications and Zimbabwean environmental/resource contexts. The material is organised as independent searchable topics so a learner can open one topic, study it in depth, then ask the offline RAG system for explanations or connections.

BIOLOGY
Cells and organisation; microscopy; nutrition; food tests; photosynthesis; digestion; respiration; gas exchange; transport in plants and humans; osmosis and diffusion; plant reproduction; human reproduction; health and disease; malaria and bilharzia; immunity and HIV; variation and inheritance; sexual and asexual reproduction; ecology and environmental applications.

CHEMISTRY
Laboratory and separation techniques; matter and particle theory; elements, compounds and mixtures; periodic classification; atomic structure; formulae and equations; mole calculations; acids, bases, pH and indicators; salts and titration; reactivity and rates; redox, combustion and corrosion; electrolysis; industrial chemistry; organic chemistry, fuels and polymers.

PHYSICS
Measurement and SI units; data and graphs; motion and forces; moments and machines; work, energy and power; heat transfer; light and sound; pressure and fluids; magnetism and electromagnetism; static electricity; electric circuits; resistance, power and energy; domestic electricity; generation and transmission; robotics and sensors; energy resources and sustainability.

PRACTICAL AND EXAMINATION SKILLS
Learners should be able to identify variables, plan fair tests, use apparatus safely, measure accurately, record observations, process results, draw and interpret graphs, evaluate methods and communicate scientific explanations.

SOURCE NOTE
The curriculum basis is the Zimbabwe School Examinations Council (ZIMSEC) O-Level Combined Science 4003 examination framework and official ZIMSEC examination resources. The explanatory notes in this Study Pack are original expanded study material intended to teach and revise the curriculum; they are not a reproduction of examination papers or a verbatim copy of a copyrighted syllabus document.

content:
COMBINED SCIENCE O-LEVEL — BIOLOGY
TOPIC: LABORATORY RULES, SAFETY AND APPARATUS

1. PURPOSE OF THE SCIENCE LABORATORY
A science laboratory is a controlled place where observations, measurements and experiments are carried out. Good laboratory practice protects learners, teachers, specimens, chemicals and equipment and makes experimental results more reliable.

2. GENERAL SAFETY RULES
• Follow the teacher's instructions and read an experiment before starting.
• Wear appropriate protective equipment when required, especially eye protection and a laboratory coat.
• Never taste chemicals. Do not deliberately smell chemicals; when directed to identify an odour, use the wafting method.
• Keep food and drinks outside the laboratory.
• Tie back long hair and secure loose clothing near flames.
• Keep benches dry and uncluttered.
• Do not run, push or play in the laboratory.
• Report broken glass, spills, burns, cuts and other accidents immediately.
• Never point a heated test tube toward yourself or another person.
• Use tongs, holders or other appropriate equipment for hot apparatus.
• Dispose of biological material, chemicals and broken glass in the correct containers.
• Wash hands after practical work.

3. COMMON APPARATUS AND USES
A beaker is used mainly for holding, mixing and heating liquids; it is not normally used for highly accurate volume measurement. A measuring cylinder measures liquid volume with greater accuracy than a beaker. A test tube holds small quantities for reactions and heating. A funnel assists transfer of liquids and can support filtration paper. An evaporating dish is used to evaporate solvent. A crucible is used for strong heating of small quantities of solids. A tripod and wire gauze support vessels above a flame. A Bunsen burner provides a controllable gas flame. A spatula transfers small quantities of solids. A balance measures mass.

4. ACCURACY IN PRACTICAL WORK
Read measuring instruments at eye level where appropriate to reduce parallax error. Record units with measurements. Repeat measurements when practical and calculate a suitable average. Distinguish accuracy, meaning closeness to the accepted value, from precision, meaning closeness of repeated measurements to one another.

1. LABORATORY ORGANISATION
Know the purpose of common apparatus: beaker for holding/mixing liquids; conical flask for mixing with reduced splashing; measuring cylinder for approximate liquid volume; pipette for transferring a measured volume; burette for delivering accurately measured variable volumes; test tube for small-scale reactions; thermometer for temperature; balance for mass; stopwatch for time; microscope for magnification; hand lens for low magnification.

2. SAFETY PRINCIPLES
Wear appropriate protective equipment, tie back long hair, keep benches clear, never taste chemicals, report spills and breakages, point heated test tubes away from people, and follow teacher instructions. Apparatus should be checked before use. Chemicals should be labelled and used in the smallest practical quantities.

3. MEASUREMENT
Read analogue scales at eye level to reduce parallax. Record a suitable number of decimal places consistent with the instrument. Repeat measurements when possible. A result that is very different from the others should be investigated as a possible anomaly.

4. VARIABLES
Independent variable = what is deliberately changed. Dependent variable = what is measured. Controlled variables = factors kept constant. A fair test changes only the independent variable while measuring the response reliably.

5. EXPERIMENTAL QUALITY
Reliability is improved by repeats and consistent procedure. Validity depends on whether the method actually tests the question. Accuracy concerns closeness to the accepted value; precision concerns closeness of repeated measurements to one another.

topic: Biology: Cells and Levels of Organisation
content:
BIOLOGY — CELLS AND LEVELS OF ORGANISATION

1. CELL THEORY AND BASIC IDEA
A cell is the basic structural and functional unit of living organisms. Organisms may consist of one cell or many cells. In a multicellular organism, cells become specialised so that different groups can perform particular functions efficiently.

2. PLANT CELL
A typical plant cell has a cellulose cell wall, cell-surface membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, a large permanent vacuole containing cell sap, and chloroplasts in photosynthetic tissues. The cell wall supports and strengthens the cell. The membrane controls movement of substances into and out of the cell. Cytoplasm contains structures and is the site of many chemical reactions. The nucleus contains genetic material and helps control cell activities. Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and absorb light energy for photosynthesis. The vacuole helps maintain cell pressure and contains dissolved substances.

3. ANIMAL CELL
A typical animal cell has a cell-surface membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus. Animal cells do not have a cellulose cell wall or chloroplasts. Small temporary vacuoles may occur in some animal cells, but they are not a defining feature of a typical animal cell.

4. SIMILARITIES AND DIFFERENCES
Both plant and animal cells possess a membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus. Plant cells generally have a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts and a large permanent vacuole; animal cells do not. These differences are related to function and lifestyle.

5. LEVELS OF ORGANISATION
Cells form tissues; tissues form organs; organs work together in organ systems; organ systems make up an organism. For example, muscle cells form muscle tissue, tissues form the heart, the heart belongs to the circulatory system, and the systems together maintain the organism.

6. SPECIALISED CELLS
A root hair cell has a long extension that increases surface area for water and mineral-ion absorption. A red blood cell is adapted to transport oxygen. A sperm cell has a flagellum for movement and many mitochondria for energy. A nerve cell has a long axon for transmitting impulses. A palisade cell contains many chloroplasts and is positioned to receive light.

1. CELL STRUCTURES
Plant cells generally have a cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, large permanent vacuole and chloroplasts. Animal cells have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus but do not normally have a cellulose cell wall or chloroplasts. Mitochondria are the main site of aerobic respiration and ribosomes are involved in protein synthesis.

2. FUNCTIONS
The nucleus contains genetic material and helps control cell activities. The cell membrane controls movement of substances into and out of the cell. Cytoplasm is where many metabolic reactions occur. Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and absorb light for photosynthesis. The vacuole contains cell sap and helps maintain turgor.

3. ORGANISATION
Similar cells form tissues; tissues form organs; organs work together in organ systems; organ systems make up an organism. Examples include muscle tissue, the heart as an organ, and the circulatory system as an organ system.

4. CELL DIFFERENTIATION
Specialised cells develop structures suited to particular functions. A root hair cell has a large surface area for absorption. A red blood cell is adapted for oxygen transport. A palisade cell contains many chloroplasts for photosynthesis.

topic: Biology: Microscopy and Biological Drawings
content:
BIOLOGY — MICROSCOPY, OBSERVATION AND SCIENTIFIC DRAWINGS

1. USING A LIGHT MICROSCOPE
Place the microscope on a stable bench and carry it with two hands. Begin with the low-power objective. Place the specimen on the stage, secure it, and use the coarse adjustment to bring the image into approximate focus. Use fine adjustment for sharp focus. Centre the important part of the specimen before changing to higher magnification.

2. MAGNIFICATION
Total magnification is calculated as:
TOTAL MAGNIFICATION = EYEPiece MAGNIFICATION × OBJECTIVE MAGNIFICATION.
For example, a 10× eyepiece with a 40× objective gives 400× total magnification.

3. FIELD OF VIEW AND MAGNIFICATION
As magnification increases, the field of view becomes smaller and the image may become dimmer. A specimen should therefore be centred before moving to high power.

4. BIOLOGICAL DRAWINGS
A good biological drawing is large, clear and made with single continuous pencil lines. Use a sharp pencil. Do not shade or use artistic colouring. Draw only structures actually seen or required. Label lines should be straight, horizontal where possible, and should not cross. Include a title and appropriate magnification when requested. If a scale is provided, use it correctly.

5. PREPARING A TEMPORARY SLIDE
A thin specimen is placed on a clean slide. A suitable drop of water or stain may be added depending on the specimen. Lower the coverslip carefully at an angle to reduce trapped air bubbles. The specimen is then viewed under low power before higher power.

6. STAINING
Many cells are almost transparent. A biological stain increases contrast so structures can be distinguished. The stain selected depends on the specimen and the structures being observed.

1. MAGNIFICATION
Total magnification = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification. If a specimen appears 40 times larger with a 10× eyepiece and 4× objective, total magnification is 40×.

2. USING A MICROSCOPE
Begin with the lowest-power objective, place the slide correctly, use coarse focus only at low power where appropriate, then fine focus for a sharp image. Increase magnification carefully. Avoid allowing the objective lens to strike the slide.

3. BIOLOGICAL DRAWINGS
Use clear single lines, no artistic shading, label with straight ruled lines, include a title and magnification where required, and draw only what is actually observed. The relative proportions of structures should be represented accurately.

4. SCALE
If an actual structure is 0.5 mm and the image is 20 mm, magnification is 20 ÷ 0.5 = 40×. Keep units consistent before calculating.

topic: Biology: Nutrition and Balanced Diet
content:
BIOLOGY — NUTRITION AND THE HUMAN DIET

1. NUTRITION
Nutrition is the taking in and use of nutrients needed for energy, growth, repair and healthy body functioning. A nutrient is a substance required by an organism for normal life processes.

2. MAJOR NUTRIENTS
Carbohydrates are major energy-providing nutrients. Starch is a storage carbohydrate found in foods such as maize, potatoes and cereals. Sugars provide readily available energy.
Proteins are needed for growth, repair and production of enzymes, hormones and other body substances. Protein sources include beans, peas, eggs, milk, fish and meat.
Fats and oils provide concentrated energy, help insulate the body and contribute to cell structures. They should not be consumed excessively.
Vitamins are required in small quantities for normal metabolism and health. Different vitamins have different functions.
Mineral salts are inorganic nutrients needed for processes such as formation of bones and teeth, nerve function and production of blood components.
Fibre is largely indigestible plant material that helps movement of food through the alimentary canal.
Water is required as a solvent, transport medium and participant in many chemical reactions.

3. BALANCED DIET
A balanced diet supplies appropriate amounts of energy, protein, fats, vitamins, mineral salts, fibre and water according to a person's needs. Requirements vary with age, activity, growth, pregnancy and health.

4. ENERGY BALANCE
Energy intake comes mainly from food. Energy is used in basal metabolism, physical activity, growth and maintaining body temperature. Persistently taking in more energy than is used can lead to excess body mass; insufficient intake can result in inadequate growth and poor health.

5. DEFICIENCY DISEASES
Lack of particular nutrients can produce deficiency disorders. Vitamin C deficiency can cause scurvy. Vitamin D deficiency can contribute to rickets in children. Iron deficiency can cause anaemia. Iodine deficiency can contribute to goitre. Protein-energy deficiency can impair growth and body function.

6. LOCAL CONTEXT
A healthy Zimbabwean diet can combine locally available foods such as maize or other cereals, beans, groundnuts, vegetables, fruits, eggs, milk and appropriate animal or fish products. Food choices should consider nutrition, affordability, availability, culture and food safety.

1. NUTRIENT FUNCTIONS
Carbohydrates provide readily available energy. Fats provide concentrated energy, insulation and energy storage. Proteins are needed for growth, repair and synthesis of enzymes, hormones and other molecules. Vitamins are required in small quantities for normal metabolism. Minerals have specific roles such as calcium in bones and teeth and iron in haemoglobin. Fibre supports normal movement of food through the gut. Water is essential as a solvent, transport medium and for metabolic reactions.

2. BALANCED DIET
A balanced diet provides appropriate amounts of nutrients and energy for age, activity and physiological needs. Excess energy intake over a long period can contribute to excessive body mass, while inadequate intake can lead to deficiency.

3. DEFICIENCY
Iron deficiency can cause anaemia because haemoglobin production is affected. Vitamin C deficiency impairs connective tissue maintenance and wound healing. Vitamin D and calcium deficiency can impair bone development. Iodine is important for thyroid hormone production.

4. FOOD AND HEALTH
Dietary advice should consider local availability and affordability. Cereals, legumes, vegetables, fruits and animal-source foods can contribute different nutrients. Food should be stored and prepared hygienically to reduce contamination.

topic: Biology: Food Tests
content:
BIOLOGY — FOOD TESTS

Food tests are simple chemical tests used to identify particular nutrients in food samples. In an examination, know the reagent, procedure, positive result and conclusion.

1. TEST FOR STARCH
Add iodine solution to the food sample. A positive test produces a blue-black colour. If the iodine remains yellow-brown, starch has not been detected.

2. TEST FOR REDUCING SUGARS
Add Benedict's solution to the sample and heat the mixture in a hot-water bath. A negative result remains blue. With increasing amounts of reducing sugar, the colour may change through green/yellow/orange to a brick-red precipitate. The exact shade depends on concentration.

3. TEST FOR PROTEIN
Add sodium hydroxide solution followed by a small amount of dilute copper(II) sulfate solution (the Biuret test). A positive result is lilac/purple.

4. TEST FOR LIPIDS
The ethanol emulsion test can be used: shake the food sample with ethanol, then add water. A positive result gives a white or cloudy emulsion.

5. FAIR TESTING
Use clean apparatus and equal-sized samples where comparisons are being made. Use controls when appropriate. Record observations before writing conclusions. A colour change is an observation; stating that a nutrient is present is the conclusion.

6. SAFETY
Chemical reagents must be handled according to laboratory instructions. Heating should be done with appropriate equipment and supervision. Never taste a sample after testing.

1. STARCH
Add iodine solution. A blue-black colour indicates starch. A yellow-brown result indicates no starch.

2. REDUCING SUGAR
Use Benedict's solution and heat the mixture safely in a hot-water bath. A positive test changes from blue through green/yellow/orange toward a brick-red precipitate depending on concentration.

3. PROTEIN
The Biuret test uses alkaline conditions and copper(II) ions. A lilac/purple colour indicates protein.

4. LIPID
The ethanol emulsion test gives a cloudy white emulsion when lipid is present.

5. FAIR TESTS
Use equal quantities of food extract and reagents where comparison is intended. Include controls where useful. State the observation first, then identify the nutrient indicated by the result.

topic: Biology: Photosynthesis
content:
BIOLOGY — PHOTOSYNTHESIS

1. DEFINITION
Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants use light energy to manufacture glucose from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen as a by-product. Chlorophyll absorbs light energy.

WORD EQUATION:
carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen
(light energy and chlorophyll are required)

2. RAW MATERIALS AND CONDITIONS
Carbon dioxide enters mainly through stomata. Water is absorbed by roots and transported through xylem. Light supplies energy. Chlorophyll absorbs the light. Temperature affects the rate because photosynthesis depends on enzyme-controlled reactions.

3. FATE OF GLUCOSE
Glucose may be used in respiration to release energy. It may be converted into starch for storage, combined with mineral ions to form other compounds such as amino acids, or used to produce cellulose and other plant materials.

4. LEAF ADAPTATIONS
Leaves usually have a large surface area to capture light. Palisade cells contain many chloroplasts. Thin leaves reduce diffusion distance. Stomata permit gas exchange. Veins supply water and transport manufactured food.

5. TESTING A LEAF FOR STARCH
A leaf is usually exposed to iodine after suitable preparation. The presence of starch is indicated by blue-black regions. A destarched plant can be used to investigate whether a factor such as light is necessary.

6. FACTORS AFFECTING RATE
Light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature can affect photosynthetic rate. When one factor is limiting, increasing another factor may have little effect until the limiting factor changes.

7. IMPORTANCE
Photosynthesis is the main entry of energy into most ecosystems and produces organic matter used by plants and organisms that feed on them. It also removes carbon dioxide and releases oxygen.

1. EQUATION
Photosynthesis converts carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen using light energy absorbed by chlorophyll. A simplified word equation is: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen.

2. LEAF ADAPTATIONS
Leaves provide a large surface area for light capture. Palisade cells near the upper surface contain many chloroplasts. Stomata allow carbon dioxide to enter and gases to leave. Veins supply water and transport manufactured sugars.

3. LIMITING FACTORS
Rate is affected by light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature. At low levels of one factor, increasing it can increase rate until another factor becomes limiting. Very high temperatures can reduce photosynthesis because enzymes and cell structures are damaged.

4. STARCH TEST
To test whether a leaf has photosynthesised, destarch the plant where required, expose selected parts to light, then test the leaf for starch using iodine after removing chlorophyll appropriately. The comparison demonstrates the requirement for light or chlorophyll depending on the design.

Photosynthesis provides chemical energy stored in organic compounds and forms the basis of food chains. It also releases oxygen and removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

topic: Biology: Digestion and the Alimentary Canal
content:
BIOLOGY — DIGESTION AND THE HUMAN ALIMENTARY CANAL

1. DIGESTION
Digestion is the breakdown of large, insoluble food molecules into small, soluble molecules that can be absorbed. Mechanical digestion changes food size without changing its chemical identity. Chemical digestion uses enzymes.

2. MAIN ORGANS
The mouth receives food and begins mechanical digestion. Saliva moistens food and contains amylase, which begins starch digestion.
The oesophagus moves food to the stomach by peristalsis.
The stomach stores and churns food. It contains hydrochloric acid, which creates an acidic environment and helps kill many microorganisms. Protease enzymes begin protein digestion.
The small intestine is the main site of chemical digestion and absorption. Bile enters from the liver and pancreatic and intestinal secretions contribute enzymes.
The large intestine absorbs water and some salts. The rectum stores faeces and the anus is the exit.

3. ENZYMES
Amylase breaks starch into smaller sugars. Proteases break proteins into amino acids. Lipases break fats into fatty acids and glycerol. Enzymes are biological catalysts and are specific to particular substrates.

4. BILE
Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder. It is alkaline and helps neutralise acidic chyme entering the small intestine. Bile emulsifies fats, breaking large fat globules into smaller droplets and increasing the surface area available to lipase.

5. ABSORPTION
The small intestine has many villi. Each villus has a large surface area and a rich blood supply. Glucose and amino acids enter blood capillaries; products of fat digestion enter mainly through the lymphatic system. The absorbed nutrients are transported to tissues for use or storage.

1. DIGESTION
Digestion is the breakdown of large, insoluble food molecules into smaller soluble molecules that can be absorbed. Mechanical digestion increases surface area; chemical digestion uses enzymes.

2. MOUTH AND STOMACH
Food is chewed and mixed with saliva. Salivary amylase begins starch digestion. In the stomach, acidic conditions support protein digestion by proteases and help limit survival of some microorganisms.

3. SMALL INTESTINE
The small intestine is the major site of chemical digestion completion and absorption. Bile from the liver emulsifies fats and helps provide suitable alkaline conditions for intestinal enzymes. Pancreatic and intestinal enzymes digest carbohydrates, proteins and fats.

4. ABSORPTION
Villi increase surface area. Their thin epithelium reduces diffusion distance and their blood supply maintains concentration gradients for absorbed soluble nutrients. Glucose and amino acids enter blood; products of lipid digestion are absorbed and transported largely through the lymphatic system before entering the bloodstream.

5. LARGE INTESTINE
Water and some ions are absorbed, leaving more solid faecal material for elimination.

topic: Biology: Respiration and Respiratory System
content:
BIOLOGY — RESPIRATION, BREATHING AND GASEOUS EXCHANGE

1. RESPIRATION
Respiration is the controlled release of energy from food molecules in cells. Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and releases more energy than anaerobic respiration.

AEROBIC WORD EQUATION:
glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy

2. ANAEROBIC RESPIRATION
Anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen. In human muscles during vigorous activity, glucose may be converted to lactic acid with a smaller energy release. In yeast, anaerobic respiration produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.

3. RESPIRATORY SYSTEM
Air enters through the nose or mouth, passes through the trachea and bronchi, then through bronchioles to alveoli in the lungs. The ribs, intercostal muscles and diaphragm change thoracic volume during breathing.

4. INHALATION
During inhalation, the diaphragm contracts and flattens; external intercostal muscles contract and move the ribs upward and outward. Thoracic volume increases, pressure falls, and air moves into the lungs.

5. EXHALATION
During normal exhalation, the diaphragm relaxes and becomes dome-shaped and the external intercostal muscles relax. Thoracic volume decreases, pressure rises and air moves out.

6. ALVEOLI
Alveoli provide a large surface area for gaseous exchange. Their walls are thin and moist, and they have a good blood supply. Oxygen diffuses from alveolar air into blood; carbon dioxide diffuses from blood into alveolar air. Ventilation and circulation maintain concentration gradients.

7. TESTS FOR RESPIRATORY GASES
Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky. Oxygen supports combustion and can relight a glowing splint under appropriate test conditions. Laboratory gas tests must be performed safely.

8. EFFECTS OF EXERCISE
Exercise increases energy demand, so respiration increases. Breathing rate and heart rate rise to deliver more oxygen and remove carbon dioxide. If oxygen supply becomes insufficient, anaerobic respiration contributes and lactic acid accumulates.

1. AEROBIC RESPIRATION
Aerobic respiration releases energy from glucose using oxygen. Word equation: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy. Energy is transferred to ATP and used for movement, active transport, synthesis and maintaining body conditions.

2. ANAEROBIC RESPIRATION
When oxygen supply is insufficient, cells can release energy anaerobically. In human muscles, glucose is converted to lactic acid with a smaller energy release. In yeast, anaerobic respiration produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.

3. GAS EXCHANGE
Air enters through the nose or mouth, passes the trachea and bronchi, then bronchioles to alveoli. Alveoli have thin walls, a large surface area and rich blood supply. These features provide efficient diffusion.

4. VENTILATION
Breathing moves air into and out of the lungs. During inhalation the diaphragm contracts and flattens, the external intercostal muscles contract, thoracic volume increases and pressure falls. During normal exhalation these changes reverse.

5. EXERCISE
During exercise, ventilation and heart rate increase so more oxygen reaches active muscles and carbon dioxide is removed more rapidly. Anaerobic respiration may contribute when oxygen delivery cannot meet demand.

topic: Biology: Transport in Plants
content:
BIOLOGY — TRANSPORT SYSTEMS IN PLANTS

1. ROOTS AND WATER UPTAKE
Root hair cells absorb water from the soil by osmosis when the soil water potential is higher than that of the cell contents. Root hairs greatly increase surface area. Mineral ions may be absorbed by active transport when uptake is against a concentration gradient.

2. XYLEM
Xylem vessels transport water and mineral ions from roots toward leaves. Mature xylem vessels are hollow, strengthened and adapted for water transport and support.

3. TRANSPIRATION
Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from a plant, mainly through stomata in leaves. Water evaporates from moist cell surfaces and diffuses out through stomata. The evaporation and movement of water help maintain a transpiration stream through xylem.

4. FACTORS AFFECTING TRANSPIRATION
Increasing light intensity usually increases transpiration because stomata tend to open for photosynthesis. Higher temperature increases evaporation and diffusion. Increased wind speed removes humid air around leaves and can increase transpiration. High humidity reduces the water-vapour gradient and usually reduces transpiration.

5. PLANT ADAPTATIONS
Plants in dry environments may have small or reduced leaves, thick waxy cuticles, sunken stomata, hairs, rolled leaves or stomata concentrated in protected areas. These features reduce water loss.

6. TENSION AND WATER MOVEMENT
Evaporation from leaves creates tension in the continuous water column. Cohesion between water molecules helps maintain the column, while adhesion assists water movement along xylem walls.

7. PLASMOLYSIS AND TURGIDITY
A plant cell in a dilute external solution may gain water and become turgid. In a concentrated solution it may lose water, causing the cell membrane to pull away from the cell wall; this is plasmolysis.

1. XYLEM
Xylem transports water and mineral ions from roots toward leaves. Mature xylem vessels are hollow and strengthened with lignin, providing a continuous pathway and support.

2. PHLOEM
Phloem transports dissolved products of photosynthesis, especially sucrose, between sources and sinks. This movement is called translocation. It can occur in different directions in different sieve-tube elements according to source and sink relationships.

3. TRANSPIRATION
Water evaporates from moist mesophyll surfaces and diffuses out through stomata. This creates a pull that contributes to movement of water through xylem.

4. FACTORS
Increasing light, temperature and wind can increase transpiration under many conditions; high humidity generally reduces it. Stomatal opening is controlled by guard cells.

5. ROOT ABSORPTION
Root hairs increase surface area. Water enters mainly by osmosis while mineral ions may enter by active transport when energy is required to move ions against a concentration gradient.

topic: Biology: Transport in Humans and Blood
content:
BIOLOGY — BLOOD, BLOOD VESSELS AND CIRCULATION

1. FUNCTIONS OF BLOOD
Blood transports oxygen, carbon dioxide, nutrients, hormones, heat and waste products. It also contributes to defence and clotting.

2. COMPONENTS
Red blood cells contain haemoglobin and transport oxygen. Their biconcave shape provides a large surface area and they lack a nucleus when mature, leaving more space for haemoglobin.
White blood cells defend against pathogens. Some engulf pathogens by phagocytosis; others produce antibodies or coordinate immune responses.
Platelets are cell fragments involved in clot formation.
Plasma is the liquid component carrying dissolved substances and transporting cells.

3. BLOOD VESSELS
Arteries carry blood away from the heart and generally have thick muscular and elastic walls because blood pressure is high. Veins carry blood toward the heart and have thinner walls and valves that help prevent backflow. Capillaries are microscopic vessels with very thin walls, allowing exchange between blood and tissues.

4. THE HEART
The right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs; the left side pumps oxygenated blood to the body. Valves help ensure one-way flow. The heart muscle contracts rhythmically and receives its own blood supply through coronary vessels.

5. DOUBLE CIRCULATION
Pulmonary circulation carries blood between heart and lungs. Systemic circulation carries blood between heart and the rest of the body. Double circulation permits efficient delivery of oxygenated blood at suitable pressure.

6. EXERCISE
During exercise, muscles require more oxygen and nutrients and produce more carbon dioxide and heat. Heart rate and cardiac output increase, improving delivery and removal.

1. DOUBLE CIRCULATION
The pulmonary circulation carries blood between heart and lungs. The systemic circulation carries blood between heart and the rest of the body.

2. HEART
The venae cavae enter the right atrium; the right ventricle pumps blood through the pulmonary artery. Pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood to the left atrium; the left ventricle pumps it through the aorta. Valves prevent backflow. The left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall because it pumps around the whole body.

3. BLOOD VESSELS
Arteries have thick muscular elastic walls for high pressure. Veins have thinner walls and valves. Capillaries have walls one cell thick, allowing rapid exchange.

4. BLOOD COMPONENTS
Red cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin. White cells defend against pathogens. Platelets support clotting. Plasma transports dissolved nutrients, hormones, carbon dioxide and waste products and distributes heat.

5. EXERCISE
Cardiac output rises as heart rate and stroke volume increase. Blood flow is redistributed toward active tissues.

topic: Biology: Osmosis and Diffusion
content:
BIOLOGY — DIFFUSION AND OSMOSIS

1. DIFFUSION
Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration due to random particle movement. It does not require cellular energy. The rate can increase with a larger concentration gradient, higher temperature and larger surface area, while a shorter diffusion distance also favours faster movement.

2. EXAMPLES
Oxygen diffuses from alveoli into blood. Carbon dioxide diffuses from tissues into blood and from blood into alveoli. Carbon dioxide enters leaves through stomata for photosynthesis.

3. OSMOSIS
Osmosis is the net movement of water molecules through a selectively permeable membrane from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential. The membrane permits water movement but restricts at least some solute particles.

4. PLANT CELLS
In dilute solution, water enters a plant cell and it becomes turgid. In concentrated solution, water leaves and the cell may become flaccid or plasmolysed.

5. EXPERIMENTAL INVESTIGATION
Potato cylinders can be placed in solutions of different concentrations. Measure initial and final mass, calculate percentage change and compare results. Control variables include cylinder size, time, temperature and volume of solution.

6. DISTINGUISHING THE PROCESSES
Diffusion can involve many particle types and does not specifically require a membrane. Osmosis specifically concerns water movement through a selectively permeable membrane. Both are passive processes.

1. DIFFUSION
Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration due to random motion. It does not require cellular energy.

2. OSMOSIS
Osmosis is the net movement of water molecules through a partially permeable membrane from higher water potential, usually a more dilute solution, toward lower water potential, usually a more concentrated solution.

3. FACTORS
A steeper concentration or water-potential gradient, higher temperature within safe limits, larger surface area and shorter diffusion distance can increase rate.

4. PLANT CELLS
A plant cell in dilute solution gains water and becomes turgid. In concentrated solution it loses water; the membrane may pull away from the cell wall, producing plasmolysis.

5. ANIMAL CELLS
Animal cells lack a rigid cell wall. In a very dilute solution, water entry can cause swelling and lysis; in a concentrated solution, water loss causes the cell to shrink.

6. ACTIVE TRANSPORT
Active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration and membrane proteins. It is different from diffusion and osmosis.

topic: Biology: Reproduction in Plants
content:
BIOLOGY — REPRODUCTION IN FLOWERING PLANTS

1. FLOWER AS A REPRODUCTIVE STRUCTURE
The stamen is the male reproductive structure and consists of anther and filament. Anthers produce pollen grains containing the male gamete nuclei. The carpel/pistil is the female reproductive structure and includes stigma, style and ovary. Ovules occur inside the ovary and contain the female gamete.

2. POLLINATION
Pollination is transfer of pollen from anther to stigma. Self-pollination occurs within the same plant; cross-pollination occurs between flowers on different plants of the same species.

3. WIND- AND INSECT-POLLINATED FLOWERS
Insect-pollinated flowers often have conspicuous petals, scent, nectar and sticky or rough pollen. Their anthers and stigmas are positioned to contact visiting insects.
Wind-pollinated flowers often have exposed anthers, long or feathery stigmas and large quantities of light pollen. Petals may be reduced and there is little need for scent or nectar.

4. FERTILISATION
After a pollen grain germinates on a compatible stigma, a pollen tube grows through the style to an ovule. The male nucleus travels down the tube and fuses with the female nucleus. The fertilised egg develops into an embryo.

5. SEED AND FRUIT
After fertilisation, the ovule develops into a seed and the ovary usually develops into a fruit. A seed contains an embryo, food reserves and a protective seed coat.

6. SEED DISPERSAL
Seeds may be dispersed by wind, water, animals, explosive mechanisms or human activity. Dispersal reduces competition with the parent plant and can help colonise new areas.

7. GERMINATION
Seeds require suitable conditions. Common requirements are water, oxygen and a suitable temperature. Light is not universally required for germination. The embryo uses stored food until the seedling becomes photosynthetically active.

1. FLOWER STRUCTURES
The stamen consists of anther and filament. The carpel includes stigma, style and ovary. Sepals protect the developing flower; petals may attract pollinators.

2. POLLINATION
Pollination is transfer of pollen from anther to stigma. It may be self-pollination or cross-pollination. Wind-pollinated flowers commonly have exposed anthers and stigmas and produce abundant lightweight pollen. Insect-pollinated flowers often have attractive petals, scent, nectar and sticky pollen.

3. FERTILISATION
A pollen tube grows toward the ovule and delivers male gamete nuclei. Fertilisation produces a zygote. The ovule develops into a seed and the ovary develops into a fruit.

4. SEED GERMINATION

BIOLOGY — HUMAN REPRODUCTION, PUBERTY AND PREGNANCY

1. MALE REPRODUCTIVE SYSTEM
The testes produce sperm and testosterone. The scrotum helps maintain a suitable temperature for sperm production. Sperm pass through ducts and are mixed with fluids from accessory glands to form semen. The penis transfers semen during sexual intercourse.

2. FEMALE REPRODUCTIVE SYSTEM
The ovaries release ova and produce hormones. The oviducts provide a route in which fertilisation may occur. The uterus is where an embryo develops. The cervix forms the lower opening of the uterus and the vagina is the birth canal.

3. PUBERTY
Puberty is the period when hormonal changes lead to sexual maturity. Changes differ between individuals. In males, testosterone promotes sperm production and changes such as voice deepening and increased body hair. In females, ovarian hormones contribute to development of reproductive maturity and the menstrual cycle.

4. MENSTRUAL CYCLE
The menstrual cycle involves coordinated changes in the ovary and uterus. An egg develops and is released at ovulation. If fertilisation does not occur, hormone levels change and the uterine lining is shed as menstruation.

5. FERTILISATION AND PREGNANCY
Fertilisation occurs when a sperm nucleus fuses with an egg nucleus. The resulting zygote divides and develops into an embryo. Implantation occurs when the developing embryo becomes embedded in the uterine lining.

6. PLACENTA AND UMBILICAL CORD
The placenta allows exchange of oxygen, nutrients and waste products between maternal and fetal blood supplies without normally mixing the two blood systems directly. The umbilical cord connects the fetus to the placenta.

7. CARE DURING PREGNANCY
Good antenatal care, balanced nutrition, appropriate medical monitoring and avoidance of harmful substances support maternal and fetal health. A pregnant person should seek qualified healthcare advice for illness, medication and complications.

BIOLOGY — HEALTH, HYGIENE AND DISEASE

1. HEALTH
Health involves physical, mental and social wellbeing. A healthy person needs adequate nutrition, clean water, sanitation, safe living conditions, physical activity, rest and appropriate healthcare.

2. PERSONAL HYGIENE
Regular bathing, handwashing, oral hygiene, clean clothing and safe food handling reduce transmission of pathogens. Hands should be washed after using the toilet, before preparing or eating food, and after contact with potentially contaminated materials.

3. WASTE DISPOSAL
Waste should be separated and disposed of safely. Appropriate methods include collection, controlled burial/landfill, composting of suitable organic waste, recycling, treatment and safe incineration where facilities meet safety requirements. Poor waste disposal can contaminate water and create breeding sites for disease vectors.

4. PATHOGENS
A pathogen is an organism or biological agent capable of causing disease. Bacteria, viruses, fungi and protozoa include important pathogens. Diseases may be communicable or non-communicable.

5. TRANSMISSION
Diseases may spread through contaminated food or water, droplets, direct contact, sexual contact, blood, vectors such as mosquitoes, or contaminated objects. Control measures interrupt transmission pathways.

6. PREVENTION
Vaccination, hand hygiene, sanitation, safe water, food hygiene, vector control, appropriate use of protective barriers and prompt treatment all contribute to disease control. Antibiotics are effective against susceptible bacteria, not viruses.

3. PREVENTION

BIOLOGY — MALARIA, BILHARZIA, TYPHOID, CHOLERA AND OTHER DISEASES

1. MALARIA
Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites and transmitted by infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. Parasites enter the bloodstream through a mosquito bite and undergo stages in humans before another mosquito acquires parasites while feeding.
Typical symptoms include fever, chills, sweating, headache, weakness and other illness signs. Severe malaria can be life-threatening. Prevention includes reducing mosquito breeding sites, using appropriate bed nets, reducing exposure to mosquito bites and following public-health measures. Diagnosis and treatment should be obtained from qualified health services.

2. BILHARZIA
Bilharzia (schistosomiasis) is caused by parasitic worms. People can become infected when larval stages in contaminated freshwater penetrate the skin. Freshwater snails act as intermediate hosts in the parasite life cycle. Prevention includes avoiding unsafe freshwater exposure in affected areas, improving sanitation, controlling transmission and obtaining recommended treatment through health services.

3. TYPHOID
Typhoid is a bacterial disease commonly associated with ingestion of food or water contaminated with faecal material. Prevention depends on safe water, sanitation, hand hygiene, food hygiene and appropriate public-health measures.

4. CHOLERA
Cholera is an acute intestinal infection associated with contaminated food or water. Profuse watery diarrhoea can cause dangerous dehydration. Prevention focuses on safe water, sanitation and hygiene. Suspected cases need urgent professional medical care because dehydration can become severe.

5. EBOLA
Ebola is a severe viral disease. Transmission can occur through contact with infected body fluids and contaminated materials. Infection prevention requires strict public-health measures and professional clinical management.

6. NON-COMMUNICABLE HEALTH RISKS
Tobacco smoke can damage the respiratory and cardiovascular systems. Excessive alcohol use can impair judgement and damage organs. Cannabis, mandrax and inhalation of solvents can have harmful effects on the brain, behaviour and other body systems. Health education should emphasise informed decisions, prevention and access to appropriate support.

Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites and transmitted by infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. The parasite undergoes stages in the human host and mosquito vector. Prevention focuses on reducing mosquito bites and controlling mosquito populations.

2. BILHARZIA
Schistosomiasis is caused by parasitic flatworms. Human infection is associated with contact with contaminated freshwater where suitable snail intermediate hosts maintain the life cycle. Safe water, sanitation and control measures reduce transmission.

3. DISEASE TRANSMISSION
Learn each disease by its causative organism, mode of transmission, symptoms at an appropriate level, prevention and control.

4. LOCAL APPLICATION
In Zimbabwe, public-health measures include vector control, sanitation, clean water provision, community education, early diagnosis and appropriate treatment.

BIOLOGY — IMMUNITY AND HIV/AIDS

1. IMMUNE DEFENCE
The body has physical and chemical barriers such as skin, mucus and stomach acid. White blood cells provide internal defence. Some engulf pathogens; other lymphocytes produce antibodies or coordinate immune responses.

2. ANTIBODIES
Antibodies are proteins produced by particular white blood cells in response to foreign substances such as antigens. Antibodies are specific and can help neutralise pathogens or mark them for destruction.

3. VACCINATION
A vaccine exposes the immune system to harmless forms or components associated with a pathogen, stimulating memory cells. If the person later encounters the pathogen, the secondary response can be faster and stronger. Vaccination is an important population-level disease-control measure.

4. HIV
HIV is a virus that attacks cells important to immune function. Without effective treatment, immune damage can progress and make a person more vulnerable to opportunistic infections.

5. AIDS
AIDS refers to a stage of advanced HIV-related immune system damage. Modern antiretroviral treatment can suppress HIV and substantially improve health and lifespan. HIV is not spread by ordinary social contact such as sharing a classroom, shaking hands or sitting beside someone.

6. PREVENTION AND SUPPORT
Prevention includes avoiding exposure to infected blood and body fluids, using appropriate healthcare and public-health measures, and obtaining accurate information. HIV testing and treatment services should be accessed through qualified health providers. Stigma and discrimination do not help disease control; people living with HIV deserve dignity and appropriate care.

1. IMMUNE DEFENCE
The body has physical barriers such as skin and mucous membranes and internal defences involving white blood cells. Phagocytes engulf pathogens. Lymphocytes can produce antibodies specific to antigens.

2. IMMUNITY
Vaccination exposes the immune system to a safe form or component associated with a pathogen so memory cells can develop. On later exposure, the secondary response can be faster and stronger.

3. HIV
HIV infects cells involved in immune defence. Without effective management, progressive damage to the immune system can increase susceptibility to opportunistic infections.

4. TRANSMISSION AND PREVENTION
HIV can be transmitted through infected blood, sexual exposure and from mother to child under certain circumstances. It is not spread by ordinary casual contact such as sharing classroom space, hugging or using the same utensils. Prevention includes informed choices, appropriate medical care, safe blood practices and professional health advice.

BIOLOGY — VARIATION AND BASIC INHERITANCE

1. VARIATION
Variation means differences between individuals of the same species. Environmental variation can result from factors such as diet, climate, exercise and disease. Genetic variation results from differences in inherited genetic material.

2. CONTINUOUS VARIATION
Continuous variation shows a range with many intermediate values, such as height or mass. It is often influenced by several genes and the environment.

3. DISCONTINUOUS VARIATION
Discontinuous variation places individuals into distinct categories, often determined strongly by genetic factors. Examples may include particular inherited blood-group categories.

4. GENES AND ALLELES
A gene is a section of DNA associated with a particular characteristic. Alternative forms of a gene are alleles. An organism receives genetic material from its parents.

5. DOMINANT AND RECESSIVE ALLELES
In a simple genetic cross, a dominant allele is expressed in a heterozygote, whereas a recessive allele is expressed when no dominant allele is present. Genotype describes allele combination; phenotype describes observable characteristics.

6. SIMPLE GENETIC CROSSES
Use symbols consistently. For a monohybrid cross, identify parental genotypes, determine gametes, combine them in a genetic diagram and state expected genotype and phenotype ratios. Ratios are probabilities for large populations, not guarantees for individual offspring.

7. ENVIRONMENT AND PHENOTYPE
Phenotype results from genetic information interacting with the environment. Therefore individuals with similar genetic backgrounds can differ when environments differ.

1. GENES AND ALLELES
A gene is a section of DNA associated with a characteristic. Alternative forms are alleles. Genotype refers to genetic constitution; phenotype is the observable characteristic produced by genotype and environmental influences.

2. INHERITANCE
During meiosis, chromosomes are separated into gametes. Fertilisation restores the diploid chromosome number and combines genetic information from two parents in sexual reproduction.

3. DOMINANT AND RECESSIVE
A dominant allele can affect phenotype when present in one copy; a recessive allele normally affects phenotype only when no dominant allele is present in the relevant simple inheritance model.

4. VARIATION
Mutation creates new alleles. Meiosis and fertilisation create new combinations. Environmental conditions can also influence phenotype.

5. NATURAL SELECTION
Individuals vary; some inherited variants improve survival or reproductive success in a particular environment; those individuals are more likely to pass on the associated alleles. Over generations, allele frequencies can change.

content:
BIOLOGY — ASEXUAL AND SEXUAL REPRODUCTION

1. ASEXUAL REPRODUCTION
Asexual reproduction involves one parent and does not require fusion of gametes. Offspring are genetically very similar to the parent, apart from changes caused by mutation. Examples include vegetative propagation in plants, binary fission in some microorganisms and budding in some organisms.

2. SEXUAL REPRODUCTION
Sexual reproduction involves the formation and fusion of gametes. In flowering plants this involves pollen and ovules; in humans it involves sperm and ova. Sexual reproduction creates genetic variation because genetic material from two parents is combined.

3. ADVANTAGES OF ASEXUAL REPRODUCTION
It can be rapid, requires one parent and can produce many offspring in a short time. A successful genotype can be copied efficiently in a stable environment.

4. DISADVANTAGES
Low genetic variation can make a population more vulnerable if environmental conditions change or a new disease appears.

5. SEXUAL REPRODUCTION
It is generally slower and requires greater biological investment, but variation can increase the chance that some offspring survive changing environmental conditions.

6. VEGETATIVE PROPAGATION
Natural methods include runners, bulbs, tubers and rhizomes. Artificial methods include cuttings, grafting and tissue culture. Vegetative propagation can preserve desirable characteristics of a crop plant.

1. ASEXUAL REPRODUCTION
Asexual reproduction involves one parent and does not involve fusion of gametes. Offspring are usually genetically very similar to the parent except for mutations. Methods include binary fission, budding, vegetative propagation and spore formation depending on the organism.

2. SEXUAL REPRODUCTION
Sexual reproduction involves fusion of male and female gametes. It generates genetic variation because genetic material from two parents is combined.

3. COMPARISON
Asexual reproduction is rapid and can be advantageous in stable environments because successful genotypes are reproduced quickly. Sexual reproduction is slower and requires gametes, but variation can improve adaptability when conditions change.

topic: Chemistry: Separation Techniques
content:
CHEMISTRY — SEPARATION TECHNIQUES

1. WHY SEPARATE MIXTURES?
A mixture contains two or more substances that are not chemically bonded. Separation methods exploit differences in physical properties such as particle size, density, magnetism, boiling point or solubility.

2. FILTRATION
Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid. The mixture is poured through filter paper. The liquid that passes through is the filtrate; the solid retained is the residue. Example: separating sand from water.

3. DECANTING
After a solid settles, the liquid above it can be carefully poured away. Decanting is less complete than filtration and is useful when rapid separation is acceptable.

4. MAGNETIC SEPARATION
Magnetic materials such as iron can be separated from non-magnetic materials using a magnet. The method is useful for mixtures containing magnetic metals.

5. WINNOWING
Winnowing uses differences in mass and aerodynamic behaviour to separate lighter particles from heavier particles, traditionally in grain processing. Wind or moving air carries lighter material farther.

6. EVAPORATION
Evaporation removes solvent from a solution to obtain a dissolved solid. Heating increases the rate of evaporation. If the solvent is valuable, distillation is more appropriate because the vapour can be condensed and collected.

7. DISTILLATION
Simple distillation separates a solvent from dissolved substances by boiling and condensing. The liquid with the lower boiling point is generally collected as distillate.

8. FRACTIONAL DISTILLATION
Fractional distillation separates miscible liquids with different boiling points. A fractionating column provides repeated evaporation and condensation, allowing components with different boiling points to separate more effectively.

9. PAPER CHROMATOGRAPHY
Chromatography separates dissolved substances according to their interactions with the stationary paper and moving solvent. A mixture forms separate spots. The Rf value is calculated as distance travelled by solute divided by distance travelled by solvent front.

1. FILTRATION
Used to separate an insoluble solid from a liquid. The solid retained is residue; liquid passing through is filtrate.

2. EVAPORATION AND CRYSTALLISATION
Evaporation removes solvent. Crystallisation obtains a dissolved solid by concentrating a solution and allowing crystals to form.

3. SIMPLE DISTILLATION
Separates a solvent from a solution by vaporising and condensing the component with the lower boiling point when appropriate.

4. FRACTIONAL DISTILLATION
Separates miscible liquids with different boiling points. A fractionating column provides repeated vaporisation and condensation, improving separation.

5. CHROMATOGRAPHY
Components distribute differently between stationary and mobile phases. A component that travels further has a larger Rf value under the same conditions. Rf = distance travelled by solute ÷ distance travelled by solvent front.

6. PURITY
A pure substance has characteristic melting or boiling behaviour. A mixture often melts or boils over a range.

content:
CHEMISTRY — MATTER AND PARTICLE THEORY

1. STATES OF MATTER
Solids have fixed shape and volume because particles are closely packed and held by strong forces. Liquids have fixed volume but take the shape of their container because particles can move past one another. Gases have neither fixed shape nor fixed volume because particles are far apart and move freely.

2. KINETIC THEORY
Particles in matter are in constant motion. Increasing temperature increases average kinetic energy. Changes of state occur when energy is transferred into or out of a substance.

3. CHANGES OF STATE
Melting is solid to liquid. Freezing is liquid to solid. Evaporation and boiling are liquid to gas. Condensation is gas to liquid. Sublimation is direct solid-to-gas change. Deposition is direct gas-to-solid change.

4. EVAPORATION AND BOILING
Evaporation occurs at the surface and can occur below the boiling point. Boiling occurs throughout a liquid at its boiling point when bubbles form. Evaporation causes cooling because higher-energy particles escape from the surface.

5. DIFFUSION
Gas particles diffuse because of random motion. Diffusion is generally faster at higher temperatures and for smaller, lighter particles, assuming comparable conditions.

6. PRESSURE
Gas pressure results from collisions of particles with container walls. Increasing temperature at constant volume increases particle kinetic energy and generally increases pressure. Compressing a gas increases collision frequency and pressure when temperature is controlled.

1. PARTICLE MODEL
Solids have closely packed particles vibrating about fixed positions. Liquids have particles close together but able to move past each other. Gases have particles far apart and moving rapidly in random directions.

2. CHANGES OF STATE
Melting, boiling, evaporation, condensation, freezing and sublimation involve changes in particle energy and arrangement, not creation of a new substance.

3. DIFFUSION
Particles spread from high concentration to low concentration due to random motion. Diffusion is generally faster in gases than liquids because particles are further apart and move more freely.

4. TEMPERATURE
Heating increases average kinetic energy. During a change of state, supplied energy is used mainly to overcome intermolecular attractions rather than raise temperature.

content:
CHEMISTRY — ELEMENTS, COMPOUNDS, MIXTURES AND PERIODIC TABLE

1. ELEMENTS
An element is a substance made of atoms containing the same number of protons. Elements cannot be broken down into simpler substances by ordinary chemical methods. Each element has a symbol, such as H for hydrogen, O for oxygen, Na for sodium and Fe for iron.

2. COMPOUNDS
A compound contains atoms of two or more elements chemically bonded in fixed proportions. Its properties differ from those of its constituent elements. A compound can be separated into elements only by chemical processes.

3. MIXTURES
A mixture contains substances physically combined. Components retain their own properties and can be separated by physical methods. Air, soil and many food products are mixtures.

4. ATOMIC STRUCTURE
An atom contains a small nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons. Protons are positively charged, electrons negatively charged and neutrons have no charge. In a neutral atom, proton and electron numbers are equal.

5. PERIODIC TABLE
Elements are arranged by increasing atomic number. Vertical columns are groups and horizontal rows are periods. Elements in the same group have related outer-electron arrangements and therefore often show similar chemical properties.

6. METALS AND NON-METALS
Metals are generally shiny, malleable, ductile and good conductors of heat and electricity. Many form positive ions. Non-metals generally have poorer electrical conductivity and may form negative ions or share electrons. There are exceptions.

7. REACTIVITY
The position of an element in the periodic table helps predict its behaviour. Group 1 metals become more reactive down the group; halogens generally become less reactive down their group. Noble gases have very stable outer electron arrangements and are relatively unreactive.

1. ELEMENT
An element contains atoms with the same proton number.

2. COMPOUND
A compound contains elements chemically combined in fixed proportions. Its properties differ from those of its constituent elements.

3. MIXTURE
A mixture contains substances physically combined. Components retain their own properties and can be separated by physical methods.

4. PERIODIC TABLE
Elements are arranged by proton number. Elements in the same group have related outer-electron arrangements and often similar chemical properties. Metals are generally on the left and centre; non-metals occupy much of the right side.

5. GROUPS
Group 1 metals are reactive and form +1 ions. Group 7 elements form -1 ions in simple ionic compounds and their reactivity generally decreases down the group. Group 0 noble gases are very unreactive because their outer electron shells are complete.

topic: Chemistry: Atomic Structure and Electronic Configuration
content:
CHEMISTRY — ATOMIC STRUCTURE, NUCLIDES AND ELECTRONIC CONFIGURATION

1. SUBATOMIC PARTICLES
Protons and neutrons occur in the nucleus; electrons occupy regions around the nucleus. The proton number is the atomic number. The total number of protons and neutrons is the mass number.

2. ISOTOPES
Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. They have similar chemical behaviour because their electron arrangements are the same, but some physical properties differ.

3. NUCLIDE NOTATION
An element can be represented as ^A_ZX, where A is mass number, Z is atomic number and X is the element symbol. Number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number.

4. ELECTRONIC CONFIGURATION
Electrons occupy shells or energy levels. For the first elements studied at O-Level, a simplified shell model is useful: the first shell holds up to 2 electrons and the second up to 8; subsequent arrangements depend on the element and level of study.

5. IONS
Atoms form ions by gaining or losing electrons. Metals commonly lose electrons to form positive ions; non-metals commonly gain electrons to form negative ions. The nucleus does not change during ordinary ion formation.

6. RELATION TO CHEMICAL REACTIVITY
Chemical reactions involve rearrangement of electrons, especially outer-shell electrons. Elements tend to react in ways that produce more stable electron arrangements. Ionic bonding involves attraction between oppositely charged ions; covalent bonding involves sharing electrons.

1. SUBATOMIC PARTICLES
Protons have positive charge and neutrons have no charge; both are in the nucleus. Electrons have negative charge and occupy regions around the nucleus.

2. ATOMIC NUMBER AND MASS NUMBER
Atomic number = number of protons. In a neutral atom, electrons equal protons. Mass number = protons + neutrons.

3. ISOTOPES
Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same proton number but different neutron numbers.

4. ELECTRON ARRANGEMENT
At O-Level, electron arrangement is commonly represented by shells. The arrangement helps explain group position and chemical behaviour.

5. IONS
Atoms form positive ions by losing electrons and negative ions by gaining electrons. Ionic charge follows from the difference between protons and electrons.

content:
CHEMISTRY — MOLES, FORMULAE AND EQUATIONS

1. RELATIVE ATOMIC AND FORMULA MASS
Relative atomic mass compares the mass of an atom with a standard reference. Relative formula mass is found by adding the relative atomic masses of all atoms shown in a chemical formula.

2. MOLE
The mole is the amount of substance containing a fixed number of particles, approximately 6.02 × 10^23. This number is Avogadro's constant. The mole links microscopic particles with measurable amounts of substance.

3. MOLE CALCULATIONS
For a substance:
number of moles = mass / molar mass.
Rearrangements give mass = moles × molar mass.

4. EMPIRICAL FORMULA
The empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound. To determine it from composition data, convert each element's mass or percentage to moles, divide by the smallest number of moles and multiply all ratios if necessary to obtain whole numbers.

5. MOLECULAR FORMULA
The molecular formula shows the actual number of atoms in a molecule. It is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula.

6. BALANCING EQUATIONS
Chemical equations must conserve atoms. Adjust coefficients, not chemical formula subscripts. Begin with elements appearing in fewer compounds and leave hydrogen and oxygen until later when appropriate. Check every element at the end.

7. STOICHIOMETRY
Coefficients in a balanced equation give mole ratios. Use the equation to convert from the known substance to the required substance. Always state units and identify limiting reactants where required.

1. MOLE
One mole contains approximately 6.02 × 10^23 particles. Relative formula mass is the sum of relative atomic masses in the formula.

2. MOLES FROM MASS
moles = mass ÷ molar mass.

3. EQUATIONS
Balance equations by changing coefficients only. The balanced coefficients give mole ratios.

4. EMPIRICAL FORMULA
Convert each element's mass or percentage into moles, divide by the smallest value and obtain the simplest whole-number ratio.

5. STOICHIOMETRY
Use the balanced equation to convert between moles of reactants and products. Then convert to mass, gas volume or concentration as required.

6. GAS VOLUME
Use the molar gas volume specified by the course/question conditions. Never assume a value if the question gives another condition.

content:
CHEMISTRY — ACIDS, BASES, pH AND INDICATORS

1. ACIDS
Acids are substances that produce hydrogen ions in aqueous solution. Common laboratory acids include hydrochloric acid, sulfuric acid and nitric acid. Acids can be corrosive and should be handled carefully.

2. BASES AND ALKALIS
A base reacts with an acid to form a salt. An alkali is a base that dissolves in water. Examples include sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide. Strong alkalis can be corrosive.

3. pH SCALE
The pH scale indicates acidity or alkalinity. Values below 7 are acidic, 7 is neutral and values above 7 are alkaline at ordinary school-level treatment. Lower pH means greater acidity; higher pH means greater alkalinity.

4. INDICATORS
Litmus is a simple indicator: acids turn blue litmus red and alkalis turn red litmus blue. Universal indicator gives a range of colours corresponding approximately to pH values.

5. ACID REACTIONS
Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen.
Acid + base → salt + water.
Acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide.
Acids can also react with metal oxides, which are commonly basic.

6. IDENTIFYING CARBON DIOXIDE
Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky. Hydrogen can be tested with a lighted splint, producing a characteristic 'pop' when conditions are appropriate. Such tests must be conducted safely and with small quantities.

7. NEUTRALISATION
Neutralisation is reaction between an acid and a base to form salt and water. The process is important in agriculture, medicine, industry and environmental management.

1. ACIDS
Acids produce hydrogen ions in aqueous solution. Strong acids ionise more completely than weak acids at comparable concentrations.

2. BASES AND ALKALIS
A base neutralises an acid. An alkali is a soluble base that produces hydroxide ions in water.

3. pH
The pH scale indicates acidity or alkalinity. Lower pH means greater acidity; higher pH means greater alkalinity. A change of one pH unit represents a tenfold change in hydrogen-ion concentration in the idealised scale.

4. INDICATORS
Indicators change colour over characteristic pH ranges. Universal indicator provides an approximate pH through a colour scale.

5. NEUTRALISATION
Acid + base → salt + water. Acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide. Acid + reactive metal → salt + hydrogen.

topic: Chemistry: Salts, Preparation and Titration
content:
CHEMISTRY — SALTS, PREPARATION OF SALTS AND TITRATION

1. SALTS
A salt is an ionic compound formed when the hydrogen ions of an acid are replaced by metal ions or another suitable positive ion. Examples include sodium chloride, copper(II) sulfate and zinc sulfate.

2. PREPARING A SOLUBLE SALT FROM AN ACID AND INSOLUBLE BASE
Add the insoluble base to warm acid until no more reacts and some solid remains, showing the base is in excess. Filter to remove excess solid. Heat the filtrate to concentrate it, then allow crystals to form on cooling. Filter and dry the crystals.

3. PREPARING A SALT BY PRECIPITATION
Mix suitable soluble solutions so that an insoluble salt forms. The solid precipitate is filtered, washed with distilled water and dried.

4. TITRATION
Titration determines the volume of one solution required to react exactly with a measured volume of another solution. A burette delivers variable volume accurately; a pipette measures a fixed volume accurately; a conical flask contains the reaction mixture; an indicator shows the endpoint.

5. TITRATION PROCEDURE
Rinse the burette with the solution that will fill it, fill it and remove air from the jet. Record the initial reading. Pipette a known volume of the other solution into a flask and add indicator. Run the burette solution into the flask while swirling. Near the endpoint, add it dropwise. Record the final reading and calculate titre = final reading − initial reading.

6. CONCORDANT RESULTS
Repeat the titration until closely agreeing titres are obtained. Use the concordant values to calculate a mean, excluding an obvious rough result when appropriate.

7. CALCULATIONS
Use the balanced equation to establish mole ratios. Convert volume in cm³ to dm³ by dividing by 1000, calculate moles using concentration × volume, then use the stoichiometric ratio to find the unknown concentration.

1. SOLUBLE SALT FROM INSOLUBLE BASE
Warm acid if appropriate, add excess insoluble base until no more reacts, filter, concentrate the filtrate and crystallise.

2. SOLUBLE SALT FROM ALKALI
Because both acid and alkali are soluble, use titration to determine the exact reacting volumes. Repeat without indicator when preparing a pure salt solution for crystallisation if required.

3. CARBONATE REACTIONS
Acid + carbonate produces carbon dioxide. The gas can be identified by passing it through limewater, which turns milky due to formation of calcium carbonate.

4. TITRATION
Rinse the burette with the solution it will contain, rinse the pipette with the solution being transferred, use an indicator appropriate to the reaction, record initial and final burette readings and calculate titre. Concordant titres should be close.

5. CRYSTALS
Concentrate the solution without overheating, allow it to cool, separate crystals and dry them.

CHEMISTRY — REACTIVITY SERIES AND RATE OF REACTION

1. REACTIVITY SERIES
A simplified reactivity series places metals in order of their tendency to react. Potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, carbon, zinc, iron, tin, lead, hydrogen, copper, silver and gold are commonly used in school-level comparisons, with hydrogen included as a reference point.

2. METALS AND ACIDS
Metals above hydrogen in the series can generally react with dilute acids to produce a salt and hydrogen. The further a reactive metal is above hydrogen, the more readily it tends to react, although conditions matter.

3. DISPLACEMENT
A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from its compound in solution. For example, zinc can displace copper from copper(II) sulfate.

4. RATE OF REACTION
Rate describes how quickly reactants are converted to products. It can be investigated by measuring gas volume, mass loss, colour change or another measurable quantity against time.

5. FACTORS
Higher temperature usually increases rate because particles have more kinetic energy and collide more frequently and effectively. Increasing concentration increases collision frequency. Increasing surface area of a solid exposes more particles. Catalysts increase rate without being used up overall.

6. COLLISION THEORY
Particles must collide for reaction to occur. A collision is effective when particles have enough energy and suitable orientation. Factors affecting collision frequency or the proportion of energetic collisions affect rate.

7. PRACTICAL INVESTIGATIONS
Keep variables such as mass of reactant, total volume and apparatus constant unless they are being investigated. Plot appropriate graphs, identify anomalies and explain results using particle theory.

CHEMISTRY — OXIDATION, REDUCTION, COMBUSTION AND RUSTING

1. OXIDATION
At basic O-Level level, oxidation may be described as gain of oxygen or loss of electrons. Reduction is loss of oxygen or gain of electrons. The two processes occur together in redox reactions.

2. COMBUSTION
Combustion is a chemical reaction involving rapid oxidation, usually releasing heat and often light. Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon in sufficient oxygen produces carbon dioxide and water. Incomplete combustion can produce carbon monoxide and/or soot.

3. RUSTING
Rusting is corrosion of iron in the presence of oxygen and water. Salt can accelerate corrosion by increasing electrical conductivity of the water layer. Rust is a hydrated mixture of iron(III) oxides/hydroxides rather than a single pure compound.

4. PREVENTING RUST
Barrier methods such as painting, oiling and greasing prevent contact with water and oxygen. Galvanising coats iron or steel with zinc. Sacrificial protection uses a more reactive metal that oxidises preferentially. Alloying can also improve corrosion resistance.

5. REDOX IDENTIFICATION
In an electron-based interpretation, oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain. A useful memory aid is OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain.

6. ENVIRONMENTAL IMPORTANCE
Combustion of fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide; incomplete combustion can release carbon monoxide. Corrosion causes economic losses by damaging infrastructure, vehicles, tools and machinery, making corrosion prevention important in Zimbabwean agriculture, mining, transport and construction.

3. RUSTING
Iron rusts when both oxygen and water are available. Salt or acidic conditions can accelerate corrosion. Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide.

CHEMISTRY — ELECTROLYSIS AND ELECTROPLATING

1. ELECTROLYTES
An electrolyte is a substance that conducts electricity when molten or dissolved in water because it contains mobile ions. Non-electrolytes do not provide mobile charged particles under the same conditions.

2. ELECTROLYSIS
Electrolysis uses electrical energy to drive a chemical change. The positive electrode is the anode and the negative electrode is the cathode. Positive ions move toward the cathode; negative ions move toward the anode.

3. REDOX AT ELECTRODES
Reduction occurs at the cathode and oxidation occurs at the anode. Metal ions can gain electrons at the cathode to form metal atoms. Negative ions or suitable species lose electrons at the anode.

4. ELECTROLYSIS OF COPPER(II) SULFATE
With copper electrodes, copper can be deposited at the cathode while copper dissolves at the anode, allowing copper purification or transfer. With inert electrodes, the products depend on the ions present and the relative ease of discharge.

5. ELECTROPLATING
Electroplating coats an object with a thin layer of another metal. The object being plated is usually the cathode. The plating metal is commonly the anode, and a solution containing ions of the plating metal acts as the electrolyte.

6. PURPOSES
Electroplating can improve appearance, increase resistance to corrosion, reduce wear or provide a desired surface property. The thickness and quality of a coating depend on current, time, electrolyte concentration and electrode conditions.

1. ELECTROLYTES
An electrolyte contains mobile ions and conducts electricity when molten or dissolved.

2. ELECTRODES
The cathode is the negative electrode in electrolysis and attracts cations. Reduction occurs at the cathode. The anode is positive and attracts anions. Oxidation occurs at the anode.

3. MOLTEN COMPOUNDS
In molten ionic compounds, metal ions are reduced at the cathode and non-metal ions are oxidised at the anode.

4. AQUEOUS SOLUTIONS
Water can also take part, so products depend on the ions present and their relative ease of discharge.

5. ELECTROPLATING
The object to be coated is normally the cathode. The anode may be the coating metal, and the electrolyte contains ions of that metal. Electroplating improves appearance, corrosion resistance or surface properties.

CHEMISTRY — INDUSTRIAL PROCESSES AND VALUE ADDITION

1. INDUSTRIAL CHEMISTRY
Industrial chemistry applies chemical principles to manufacture useful products at scale. Good industrial design balances yield, rate, energy use, cost, safety, environmental protection and availability of raw materials.

2. IRON EXTRACTION
Iron can be extracted from iron ore in a blast furnace. Carbon monoxide reduces iron oxides to iron. Limestone helps remove acidic impurities by forming slag. The process involves high temperatures and produces useful iron but also carbon dioxide and other emissions.

3. HABER PROCESS
The Haber process manufactures ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen:
N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3.
A suitable catalyst, elevated temperature and high pressure are used industrially. Increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules, while temperature is a compromise between equilibrium yield and reaction rate.

4. CONTACT PROCESS
The Contact process is used to manufacture sulfuric acid. Sulfur or sulfide-containing materials are oxidised to sulfur dioxide, which is converted to sulfur trioxide using a catalyst. Sulfur trioxide is then processed to produce sulfuric acid.

5. SOAP PRODUCTION
Soap can be produced by reacting fats or oils with a strong alkali. This process is called saponification. The products include soap and glycerol.

6. PEANUT BUTTER
Food processing is an example of value addition: a raw agricultural product such as groundnuts can be cleaned, roasted, milled and processed into a higher-value product. Industrial processing requires hygiene, quality control, appropriate packaging and safe storage.

7. ENVIRONMENT
Industrial processes should minimise waste, recycle useful materials where possible, treat effluent and control air emissions. Value addition can create employment and increase the economic value of Zimbabwean resources.

1. INDUSTRIAL CHEMISTRY
Industrial chemistry converts raw materials into useful products at scale. Questions should consider raw materials, process conditions, products, energy requirements, catalysts where relevant, economic value and environmental impact.

2. CEMENT AND LIMESTONE
Limestone is an important mineral resource. On heating, calcium carbonate decomposes to calcium oxide and carbon dioxide. Calcium oxide reacts with other materials in cement manufacture.

3. METAL EXTRACTION
Extraction depends on reactivity. Metals below carbon may be extracted by reduction of oxides with carbon or carbon monoxide; very reactive metals require electrolysis.

4. ENVIRONMENT
Industrial activity can create dust, gases, wastewater and solid waste. Cleaner production, recycling, treatment systems and energy efficiency reduce environmental impacts.
